submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the word that states how far a claim runs along a scale of extent: approximatives that stop just short of a bound (nearly 2.49, almost 2.41, practically 1.90, virtually 1.93, approximately 2.07, roughly 1.80 - all measured at the word's own position in my own probes), comparatives and measure words that fix an amount (most 1.69, more 2.20, less 2.02, at least 2.01, over 1.54, exactly 1.42), and scalar negation of a bound (not all 2.41, un-/unless at the scan's 2.1-2.5 peaks); it then holds a decaying trace for two to four tokens as the measured phrase is read out ('nearly all of the' = 2.49 / 1.57 / 1.16 / 0.76). It stays at or near zero on plain narrative, on clause negation in an ordinary sentence, on bare quantifiers that carry no degree word (all 0.75, some, many, none 0.89, several) and on intensifiers that merely grade a single adjective (extremely 1.26 vs almost 1.87 in the same frame).

rival_explanations: Narrower, bound-approximation reading: the pole fires only when a quantity is said to fall just short of, or exactly at, a limit (nearly, almost, practically, virtually, approximately, exactly, at least, less than), and the more/most/not/un hits are a separate weaker job, so on new text 'just under', 'close to' and 'at most' should fire as hard as 'nearly' while 'most' and 'more' should not.

Broader, hedging-and-qualification reading: the pole fires wherever the clause hedges or limits a claim, including epistemic hedges, formal disclaimers and statistical reporting prose, so 'presumably', 'possibly', 'reportedly' and 'included'/'individuals' in a study-population sentence should fire as strongly as 'nearly' (my probes put them at 0.6-1.2 against 2.4, but this reading explains the technical-prose leftovers that the hypothesis leaves open).

Lookahead reading: the pole is preparing the quantifier or measure token that comes next rather than reading the degree word - zero-ablating it removes probability mass from ' all', ' every', ' 100' and ' 1' - so it should peak one token before a quantifier even with no degree word in front, and replacing the word after the peak should leave the peak unchanged.

Immersed oil cooling for data-centres? - AnotherHustler I've seen some eccentric examples of oil cooling for desktop PCs, however this startup is doing the same thing for datacenters - http://asperitas.com/

Does anyone have any experience in this space?

Aside from cost reduction, the elephant in the room is ease of server hardware maintenance. If the dead server has been immersed in oil then it's a messy job to replace components. Also, I'm wondering about the oil itself degrading components - for example, I think oil eats network cables?

I'm wondering if this might be the next big thing? Or just a hassle? ====== chha No intimate knowledge of this, but as with anything it's the economics that will decide if this is the next big thing or not. James Hamilton did a writeup on the economics of running a datacenter a few years back[1], and concluded that approximately 1/3 of the montly expenses are for power, distribution and cooling. If immersive cooling doesn't significantly reduce the lifetime of components and doesn't add costs (additional mops?) enough to offset the reduction, there is no reason why it shouldn't be useful for most datacenters. Intel was working on this a few years back [2], and as far as I can tell the Cray 2 used immersive cooling for some components in the mid-80s. [1] - [http://perspectives.mvdirona.com/2010/09/overall-data- center...](http://perspectives.mvdirona.com/2010/09/overall-data-center- costs/) [2] - [https://www.technologyreview.com/s/429179/intel-servers- take...](https://www.technologyreview.com/s/429179/intel-servers-take-a-deep- dive-to-cool-off/) ------ brudgers Oil immersion is commonly used for transformers in power distribution systems. The cylindrical transformers on power poles are cylindrical for the same reasons beer cans are, it's a good shape for holding liquids. In commercial buildings it is also not uncommon for transformers to be immersed in oil. But oil's flammability creates substantial fire hazard and modern building codes address this by limiting the density at which the oil in transformers can be distributed; specifying fire resistant separation; and other substantial hazard mitigations as the hazard increases. Since the oil around servers burns just like the oil around transformers, there probably won't be any special exception for oil immersed servers in the building code any time soon. So I'd bet against large commodity data center installations...a state sponsored agency's data center might be another matter.

باباتي  هي بلدة في  في إقليم مانيارا في تنزانيا. هي العاصمة الإدارية لولاية باباتي الحضرية وولاية باباتي الريفية وأيضًا العاصمة الإدارية لإقليم مانيارا.

تطورت بلدة باباتي من مجرد قرية منذ إنشاء ولاية باباتي في عام 1985. عزز الوضع الجديد للمدينة النمو السريع. تقع المدينة على ارتفاع  بالقرب من نهاية  وقاعدة بحيرة باباتي أسفل .

التاريخ 
تُروى القصة أن اسم المدينة نتج عن سوء فهم مشرف أعمال طرق ألماني لصبي من الغورووا. لم يفهم الصبي السؤال الذي طرحه الألماني حول اسم الموقع. وأشار إلى رجل كبير في السن وقال "بابا تي" ، وهذا يعني في لغته "هذا والدي". سجل الألماني اسم "باباتي" لأنه يعتقد أن هذا هو اسم البلدة.

يُزعم في كتاب Tanganyikan Guerilla: East African Campaign 1914-1918 ، أن ابن نابليون، الذي كان آنذاك عقيدًا في سلاح الفرسان البريطاني، مات ودُفن في باباتي.

Starting in the 1940s
With Regard to the Inventors and Their "Fights"
by Prof Dr Randolph Riemschneider
Central Institute of Chemistry, Universidade Federal de
In the 40s and 50s, particularly in the Second World War and the Postwar Era, chemical pest control agents based on chlorine compounds of the DDT- and DIENE-groups as well as Gammexan as so-called "halocarbon class contact insecticides" (1, 2) played an important role. Thousands and thousands of publications appeared in the frame of chemical pest control research; in the fight against the “superpower insect” many harvests could be saved, illnesses like malaria be successfully contained. There were internal fights and altercations with respect to copyrights and Nobel Prize(s) related to DDT and DIENE group insecticides, latter based in hexachlorocyclopentadiene chemistry. Consideration is also given to the early references to the calculation of the use and risk in the widespread application of chemical pest control agents. -- The editor.
At the start of the 1870s the doctoral candidate O Zeidler in Stasbourg (3) synthesized - in the frame of investigations into the BAYER condensation - from 2 mol chlorobenzene and 1 mol chloral the compound C14H9Cl5, loosely known as dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (I): Fig 1. Some 70 years later the compound became interesting again when Dr P Müller - supervised by Dr P Läuger - again produced C14H9Cl5 (I) in the company labs of GEIGY AG, Basle while searching for new, effective stomach poisons. GEIGY patented I and analogues as general insecticides at the start of the 40s and brought preparations based on I onto the market under the name "Gesarol" for protecting crops and "Neozid" for combatting ectoparasites. But only the Americans recognized the actual value of I in the second world war. They coined the term DDT, derived from dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (Fig 1).
Cl3C-CHO + 2 C6H5Cl → C14H9Cl5
Cl3C-CHO + 2 C6H5Cl → C14H9Cl5 (I)
Fig 1: Synthesis of dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (I) from 1 mol chloral and 2 mol chlorobenzene [BAYER condensation] (6)
Examples of successes with DDT in WW2: the typhus epidemic, transmitted by lice, was successfully combatted in Naples in 1943; the dangers from insects (eg malaria) were considerably reduced on the Asian fronts by spraying the insects with DDT before troop landings; during and after the second world war harvests were saved by means of DDT and thus the food for many people assured.; malaria was contained worldwide with the aid of DDT and its analogues (above all DDD) and thus the lives of many people. Reasons enough to initially play down the concerns necessarily related to the widespread use of chemical toxins, when balancing the use against the risk (4a-4d).

The present invention relates to an interlocking mechanism, and more particularly to a computer enclosure interlocking mechanism by which a cover of the enclosure can be conveniently interlocked to and released from a chassis of the enclosure.
Personal computers are now part of our daily life. Our modem society is closely linked to computer on which a variety of data are processed, linked and interchanged. The computer generally comprises an enclosure configured by an enclosure and a cover assembled thereto, and a bezel which is attached to a front panel of the enclosure. The enclosure is used to carry a plurality of components which jointly configure the computer.
Generally, the cover is assembled to the chassis by screws and which takes time in assembly and disassembly. This inevitably increases the manufacturing cost. In addition, screws or the equivalents are also parts of inventory which should be carefully monitored in order to prevent a shutdown of the production line. Understandably, some attempts have been taken to introduce the snapping type enclosure by using less screws. Anyhow, forming recessions or hooks on the panels for mutually fastening complicates the corresponding manufacturing and sometimes results in unnecessary gap therebetween. The object of the invention is to provide an enclosure with the associated snap-in chassis and cover which is easy to be made with a compact structure thereof.
An object of this invention is to provide a computer enclosure in which an interlocking mechanism is provided to facilitate engagement and disengagement between cover and chassis of the enclosure.
Another object of this invention is to provide a computer enclosure in which the interlocking mechanism is arranged such that side panels of the cover and the chassis can be closely arranged to prevent EMI leakage from the enclosure.
In order to achieve the objects set forth, a computer enclosure for enclosing electrical devices therein comprises a chassis having a bottom panel and a pair of side panels with a reduced height portion adjacent to a rear panel thereof. The rear panel includes a wing fixedly attached with the reduced height portion and is coplanar to the side panel. The reduced height portion defines a recess therein. A spring latch extends downward and outward from the wing portion of the rear panel. A cover is detachably assembled to the chassis having a top panel and a pair of side panels corresponding to the side panels of the chassis. The cover includes a block received in the recess and engaged with the spring latch. when the cover is assembled to the chassis.
According to an aspect of the present invention, the cover her includes a hook interlocked to the reduced height portion.
These and additional objects, features, and advantages of the present invention will become apparent after reading the following detailed description of the preferred embodiment of the invention taken in conjunction with the appended drawings.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The farmer walked out to the barn before sunrise and fed the chickens in the dark.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Plain narrative with no degree word, the hypothesis's first inactive class; none of the three rival readings has a trigger here either.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She opened the letter, read it twice, and put it back in the drawer.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A second plain-narrative negative with different vocabulary, so the plain-prose class is tested away from farm words.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: On market day the square filled before seven. Farmers set up their stalls along the north wall, and the baker carried trays of bread from the back of his van to the counter. By nine the crowd had thickened, and the fishmonger was calling prices to people gathered around the ice. A boy wheeled a cart of apples past the fountain and stopped to tie his shoe. When the church bell rang at noon, the traders covered their produce and began to pack the crates away. The square was empty again an hour later.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long (~95-token) plain narrative length-matched to the long holdout, containing no degree word; the hypothesis predicts it stays near zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The committee did not approve the new budget at yesterday's meeting.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Clause negation in an ordinary sentence, an explicitly inactive class; the 'at' is not part of 'at least'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He never visited the museum because the trains were not running that day.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Clause negation ('never', 'not') without a scalar bound, which the hypothesis says does not fire although 'not all' does.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Some of the students arrived early, several brought notes, and many left at noon.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Bare quantifiers (some, several, many) carrying no degree word, a listed inactive class; the lookahead reading's evidence names all/every/numbers, not these.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The gate was locked for the winter.
All the paths had been cleared, and none of the lamps were lit.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Bare quantifiers 'all' and 'none' after a newline and mid-prose, an unusual position; the hypothesis predicts no firing, while the lookahead reading predicts a peak on the newline token one before ' All'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The soup was extremely hot and the bread was very stale.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Intensifiers grading single adjectives (extremely, very), the class the hypothesis pins near 1.26 and calls inert.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Her remarks were incredibly blunt, and the audience sat in absolute silence.
adversarial_test_results.detail: More adjective-grading intensifiers (incredibly, absolute) with no scale of extent, predicted inactive.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Thomas More served as Lord Chancellor of England before his execution in 1535.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'More' as a surname, the same token in a non-measure sense; the hypothesis says it fires only when the word fixes an amount.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: A small plane circled over the harbour for an hour before it landed.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Over' as a spatial preposition of place, not a measure word, so the hypothesis predicts no firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: That is exactly what I meant when I said the plan needed work.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Exactly' as emphatic agreement, fixing no amount on a scale of extent.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She read the passage once more before she answered the question.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'More' meaning 'again' rather than a comparative of amount; the hypothesis predicts this sense does not fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The most important finding was buried in an appendix at the back.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Most' as a superlative intensifier grading a single adjective, the same inert role the hypothesis assigns to 'extremely', not a measure of amount.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The board met virtually by video link because of the storm.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Virtually' meaning 'online', not an approximative stopping just short of a bound, so readings that key on the approximative sense predict no firing on it.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The boundaries were drawn roughly along the ridge above the valley.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Roughly' as a manner adverb, not an approximative of quantity; the hypothesis predicts the approximative sense is what fires.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: At least she apologized for the delay before the meeting ended.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'At least' as a consolation discourse marker with no quantity on a scale, so the hypothesis's fixing-an-amount reading predicts no firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The shipment will presumably arrive on Friday if the roads stay open.
adversarial_test_results.detail: An epistemic hedge with no extent word; the hypothesis leaves this at zero while the broader hedging-and-qualification reading predicts a hit.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The study population included individuals aged twelve years and older from local clinics.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Study-population prose ('included', 'individuals') stripped of 'unvaccinated'; the hypothesis predicts inactivity, the hedging reading predicts a hit on its own stated example.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The ushers checked that every ticket matched a seat number before the doors opened.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A bare universal quantifier 'every' preceded by 'that' with no degree word; the hypothesis predicts inactivity while the lookahead reading predicts a peak one token before ' every'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: In the survey, nearly 40 percent of the respondents said they would switch providers.
adversarial_test_results.detail: An approximative 'nearly' before a number in a new survey frame, which the hypothesis predicts fires; the hedging reading counts this as statistical-reporting prose and the lookahead peak would sit on ' nearly' itself.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: By Friday morning, almost every seat in the hall had been sold.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Almost' before a quantifier in a new frame; the hypothesis predicts a hit, the lookahead reading also predicts one token before ' every'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: By Monday morning, more than half the class had signed up for the field trip.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'More' as a comparative fixing an amount; the hypothesis predicts a hit while the bound-approximation reading says more/most should not fire, and the lookahead peak would fall on ' than'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: In this district, most households heat their homes with natural gas.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Most' as a quantity word fixing an amount; the hypothesis predicts a hit, the bound-approximation reading predicts it does not fire, and no quantifier follows ' most' for the lookahead reading to prepare.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: In the greenhouse, not all of the samples survived the winter.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Not all' as scalar negation of a bound, one of the claimed triggers, kept off the first position; the bound-approximation reading omits it, the hedging reading counts it as limiting a claim, and the lookahead reading predicts a peak on ' not' one token before ' all'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The outdoor concert will go ahead unless the storm warning is extended.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Unless' as scalar negation of a bound in a novel weather context, which the hypothesis predicts fires and the bound-approximation reading excludes.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The old mill stood unaltered for seventy years after the factory closed.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The 'un-' privative prefix in a new word, the family the hypothesis claims at the scan's 2.1-2.5 peaks; the tokens are ' un' | 'al' | 'tered', so the claimed ' un' token sits mid-probe and is measured.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: By the end of the year, close to half of the staff will have worked here a decade.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The paraphrase 'close to' approximating a quantity, absent from the top examples; the hypothesis predicts a hit, the bound-approximation reading explicitly predicts one too, and the lookahead peak would fall on ' to' before ' half'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Antes del viernes, casi todos los vecinos firmaron la petición.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Spanish 'almost all' with the degree word mid-probe; 'casi' is split into ' cas' | 'i' and followed by ' todos', which the hypothesis's language-general extent claim predicts fires and the lookahead reading also predicts one token before ' todos'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The regional water authority published its annual review on Tuesday. The report notes that the reservoir system held approximately 3.5 billion litres at the end of the wet season, which the authors describe as within the long-run average. Demand from the northern districts rose again last summer, and two of the older treatment works were shut for repairs during August. The authority plans to inspect the remaining pipelines before the winter, and it will publish a further update once the field surveys are complete.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A ~85-token water-authority report with 'approximately' deep in the passage, length-matched to the long narrative negative and testing long-context and cross-genre firing; the lookahead peak would sit on ' approximately' before the ' 3' token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The inspectors reported that nearly all of the buildings had failed the safety review last year. -> The inspectors reported that all of the buildings had failed the safety review last year.

The present invention relates to an interlocking mechanism, and more particularly to a computer enclosure. -> The present invention relates to an interlocking mechanism, and particularly to a computer enclosure.
The inspectors reported that not all of the buildings had passed the safety review last year. -> The inspectors reported that none of the buildings had passed the safety review last year.
The inspectors reported that nearly all of the buildings had failed the safety review. -> The inspectors reported that mostly all of the buildings had failed the safety review.

readings.explanation: The pole fires on the word that states how far a claim runs along a scale of extent: approximatives that stop just short of a bound (nearly 2.49, almost 2.41, practically 1.90, virtually 1.93, approximately 2.07, roughly 1.80 - all measured at the word's own position in my own probes), comparatives and measure words that fix an amount (most 1.69, more 2.20, less 2.02, at least 2.01, over 1.54, exactly 1.42), and scalar negation of a bound (not all 2.41, un-/unless at the scan's 2.1-2.5 peaks); it then holds a decaying trace for two to four tokens as the measured phrase is read out ('nearly all of the' = 2.49 / 1.57 / 1.16 / 0.76). It stays at or near zero on plain narrative, on clause negation in an ordinary sentence, on bare quantifiers that carry no degree word (all 0.75, some, many, none 0.89, several) and on intensifiers that merely grade a single adjective (extremely 1.26 vs almost 1.87 in the same frame).

Narrower, bound-approximation reading: the pole fires only when a quantity is said to fall just short of, or exactly at, a limit (nearly, almost, practically, virtually, approximately, exactly, at least, less than), and the more/most/not/un hits are a separate weaker job, so on new text 'just under', 'close to' and 'at most' should fire as hard as 'nearly' while 'most' and 'more' should not.

Broader, hedging-and-qualification reading: the pole fires wherever the clause hedges or limits a claim, including epistemic hedges, formal disclaimers and statistical reporting prose, so 'presumably', 'possibly', 'reportedly' and 'included'/'individuals' in a study-population sentence should fire as strongly as 'nearly' (my probes put them at 0.6-1.2 against 2.4, but this reading explains the technical-prose leftovers that the hypothesis leaves open).

Lookahead reading: the pole is preparing the quantifier or measure token that comes next rather than reading the degree word - zero-ablating it removes probability mass from ' all', ' every', ' 100' and ' 1' - so it should peak one token before a quantifier even with no degree word in front, and replacing the word after the peak should leave the peak unchanged.
